Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honour and power: for thou hast created all things, and for thy pleasure they are and were created –Revelation 4:11.

This hymn, often called the “National Anthem of Christendom,” is perhaps one of the greatest of hymns of all time. It was written by Edward Perronet, first appearing in the November 1779 issue of Gospel Magazine. It was edited by Augustus Toplady, who is also the author of another well-known hymn, “Rock of Ages”. The text of this hymn, All Hail the Power of Jesus Name, has been translated into almost every language where Christianity is known. Wherever it is sung, it communicates to the spiritual needs of human hearts. One writer has said, “So long as there are Christians on earth, it will continue to be sung; and after that, in heaven.”

Edward Perronet was born at Sundridge, Kent, England, in 1726. He was a descendant of a distinguished French Huguenot family who had fled to Switzerland and later to England because of the religious persecution in France. Edward’s father, a pastor in the State Church of England, was strongly sympathetic with the evangelical movement spearheaded by the Wesleys and George Whitefield. Edward, too, like his father, became a minister in the Anglican Church but was always critical of its ways. Once he wrote, “I was born and I am likely to die in the tottering communion of the Church of England, but I despise her nonsense.” Soon, however, he broke from the Church and threw himself strenuously into the evangelistic endeavors of the Wesleys during the 1740s and 1750s.

Charles Wesley writes of Edward Perronet’s boldness in preaching. At one time he and Perronet were beset in a house by a mob of rough revilers, whom Perronet opposed courageously, while they abused him and threw dirt on him. It was during this time that the Wesleys and their followers suffered much persecution and even violence from those who disagreed with their ministry. Concerning these experiences, Wesley made the following notation in his diary: “From Rockdale we went to Bolton, and soon found that the Rockdale lions were lambs in comparison with those of Bolton.” Edward Perronet was thrown down and rolled in mud and mire. Stones were hurled and windows broken.

Another interesting account is given regarding the relationship between the Wesleys and Perronet. John Wesley wanted to hear Perronet preach, and he, being 18 years younger than John had always refused to preach in the older churchman’s presence. So, one day Wesley seeing Edward in the congregation announced that he would preach at the next service. Desiring to avoid a public conflict with Wesley, Perronet mounted the pulpit the next morning, but quickly explained that he had never consented to preach. “However,” he added, “I shall deliver the greatest sermon that has ever been preached on earth.” He then read the Sermon on the Mount and sat down without comment.

After eight years of co-operation with the Wesleys, Perronet’s strong-mindedness and free spirit caused a division between them, as he disagreed with some of their regulations. They continued, however, to esteem and love each other.

The last years of Perronet were spent at Canterbury, where he was pastor of an independent church, and where he died in 1792, at the age of sixty-six. His last words have also become a classic: “Glory to God in the height of His divinity! Glory to God in the depth of His humanity! Glory to God in His all-sufficiency! Into His hands I commend my spirit.”

Though Perronet wrote many other hymns and forms of poetry, none of them, have attained fame except the immortal “All Hail the Power of Jesus Name.” The success of this text has, no doubt, been furthered by three fine tunes. “Coronation,” composed by Oliver Holden, a Massachusetts carpenter, self-taught musician, and respected singing-school teacher, is most widely used in America. “Miles Lane” composed by William Shrubsole, Perronet’s personal friend, is the most popular in Great Britain. While the festive “Diadem” tune, composed in 1838 for this text by James Ellor, an English layman, is frequently used as a choir number. This hymn was originally written having the title, “On the Resurrection,” and there were eight stanzas, as follows:

All hail the power of Jesus’ name,
Let angels prostrate fall
Bring forth the royal diadem,
To crown Him Lord of all!

Let high born seraphs tune the lyre,
And, as they tune it, fall
Before His face who tunes their choir,
And crown Him Lord of all!

Crown Him, ye morning stars of light,
Who fixed this floating ball,
Now hail the Strength of Israel’s might,
And crown Him Lord of all!

Crown Him, ye martyrs of your God,
Who from His altar call;
Extol the stem of Jesse’s rod,
And crown Him Lord of all!

Ye seed of Israel’s chosen race,
Ye ransomed of the fall,
Hail Him who saves you by His grace
And crown Him Lord of all!

Hail Him, ye heirs of David’s line,
Whom David Lord did call.
The God incarnate, Man divine,
And crown Him Lord of all!

Sinners, whose love can ne’er forget
The wormwood and the gall,
Go spread your trophies at His feet,
And crown Him Lord of all!

Let every tribe and every tongue
That bound creation’s call
Now shout in universal song,
The crowned Lord of all!

As it now stands in our hymnbooks, the hymn is shortened and changed, and one stanza has been added by the famous hymn collector, Rev. John Rippon, in 1787.

Oh, that with yonder sacred throng
We at His feet may fall;
We’ll join the everlasting song,
And crown Him Lord of all.

As we wrap up this amazing story of the life of Edward Perronet and the others who have had their part in bringing this immortal hymn to us, let’s take a look in closing at the effect this hymn has had on heathens who knew nothing about Jesus. The most famous story connected with Perronet’s great hymn is told of the missionary to India, Rev. E.P. Scott. One day he saw on the street a man of so strange an appearance that he inquired about him and learned that he belonged to a wild mountain tribe among whom Christ had never been preached. Mr. Scott prayed over the matter and decided to visit that tribe. As soon as he reached their mountain home, he fell in among a savage band of murderous tribesmen who were on a war expedition, and who were closing in on him with their spears. They seized him and pointed their spears at his heart. At once the missionary drew out the violin that he always carried with him and began to play and sing in the native language, “All hail the power of Jesus’ name!” He closed his eyes, expecting death at any minute. When he reached the fourth stanza, and nothing had happened, he opened his eyes, and was amazed to see that the spears had fallen from the hands of the savages, and big tears were in their eyes! They invited Mr. Scott to their homes, and he spent the remaining years of his life preaching and ministering God’s love and redemption to these people. God in His providence used a simple hymn as a means of introducing the gospel to a group of needy pagans.

U iswaardig, Here, om heerlikheid en eer en krag te ontvang: want U het alle dinge geskape, en om U wil het hulle bestaan en is geskape – Openbaring 4:11.

Hierdie hy lied, dikwels die “Nasionale Volkslied van die Christendom” genoem, is miskien een van die grootste liedere van alle tye. Dit is deur Edward Perronet geskryf en verskyn die eerste keer in die November 1779-uitgawe van Gospel Magazine. Dit is geredigeer deur Augustus Toplady, wat ook die skrywer is van ’n ander bekende gesang, “Rock of Ages”. Die teks van hierdie gesang, All Hail the Power of Jesus Name, is in byna elke taal vertaal waar Christusendom bekend is. Waar dit ook al gesing word, spreek dit die geestelike behoeftes van mense se harte aan. Een skrywer het gesê: “Solank daar Christene op aarde is, sal dit aanhou gesing word; en daarna, in die hemel.”

Edward Perronet is in 1726 by Sundridge, Kent, Engeland gebore. Hy was ’n afstammeling van ’n vooraanstaande Franse Hugenote-familie wat na Switserland en later na Engeland gevlug het weens die godsdienstige vervolging in Frankryk. Edward se vader, ’n predikant in die State Church of England, was sterk simpatiek met die evangeliese beweging wat deur die Wesleys en George Whitefield aangevoer is. Edward het, soos sy vader, ook ’n predikant in die Anglikaanse Kerk geword, maar was altyd kritiek op haar maniere. Eenkeer het hy geskryf: “Ek is gebore en waarskynlik sal ek in die wankelende gemeenskap van die Church of England sterf, maar ek minag haar nonsens.” Binnekort het hy egter van die Kerk losgemaak en hom kragtig in die evangeliserende bedrywighede van die Wesleys in die 1740’s en 1750’s gewerp.

Charles Wesley skryf van Edward Perronet se moedigheid in prediking. Op een stadium is hy en Perronet in ’n huis deur ’n skare van ruwe lasteraars aangeval, wat Perronet dapper teëgestaan het terwyl hulle hom beledig en met modder bedek het. Dit was in hierdie tyd dat die Wesleys en hul volgelinge baie vervolging en selfs geweld van diegene wat nie met hul bediening saamgestem het nie, ervaar het. Oor hierdie ervarings het Wesley die volgende aantekening in sy dagboek gemaak: “Van Rockdale het ons na Bolton gegaan, en het gou gevind dat die Rockdale-luie lammetjies was in vergelyking met dié van Bolton.” Edward Perronet is neergeslaan en in modder en drab gerol. Stene is gegooi en vensters gebreek.

’n Ander interessante verslag handel oor die verhouding tussen die Wesleys en Perronet. John Wesley wou Perronet hoor preek, en hy, wat 18 jaar jonger as John was, het altyd geweier om in die ouer kerkmans teenwoordigheid te preek. Op ’n dag, toe Wesley Edward in die gemeente sien, het hy aangekondig dat hy by die volgende diens sal preek. Om ’n openbare konflik met Wesley te vermy, het Perronet die volgende oggend die kansel bestyg, maar vinnig verduidelik dat hy nooit ingestem het om te preek nie. “Tog,” het hy bygevoeg, “ek sal die grootste preek doen wat nog ooit op aarde gepreek is.” Hy het toe die Bergpredikant gelees en sonder kommentaar gaan sit.

Na agt jaar van samewerking met die Wesleys, het Perronet se stewige geaardheid en vrye gees ’n skeiding tussen hulle veroorsaak, omdat hy met sommige van hul regulasies verskil het. Hulle het egter voortgegaan om mekaar te ag en lief te hê.

Die laaste jare van Perronet is in Canterbury deurgebring, waar hy predikant van ’n onafhanklike kerk was, en waar hy in 1792 op sestig-en-sesjarige ouderdom gesterf het. Sy laaste woorde het ook ’n klassieke status verkry: “Eer aan God in die hoogte van Sy godheid! Eer aan God in die diepte van Sy mensheid! Eer aan God in Sy algenoegsaamheid! In Sy hande beveel ek my gees aan.”

Alhoewel Perronet baie ander gesange en vorme van poësie geskryf het, het geen van hulle roem verwerf behalwe die onsterflike “All Hail the Power of Jesus Name.” Die sukses van hierdie teks is, sonder twyfel, verder bevorder deur drie uitstekende melodieë. “Coronation,” deur Oliver Holden gekomponeer — ’n Massachusets-houtbewerker, selfopgeleide musikant en gerespekteerde sangskoolonderwyser — word in Amerika die wydste gebruik. “Miles Lane,” gekomponeer deur William Shrubsole, Perronet se persoonlike vriend, is die gewildste in Groot-Brittanje. Terwyl die feestelike “Diadem”-melodie, in 1838 vir hierdie teks deur James Ellor, ’n Engelse lekmens, gekomponeer, dikwels as ’n koornommer gebruik word. Hierdie gesang is oorspronklik onder die titel “On the Resurrection” geskryf en het agt stanzaʼs gehad, soos volg:

Ere aan die Naam van Jesus toe!
Laat engele nederig val,
Bring die koninklike diadeem voort,
Om Hom te kroon, Here van almal!

Laat hooggeborene serafe die lier stem,
En terwyl hulle dit stem, val neer
Voor Sy aangesig wat hul koor stem,
En kroon Hom, Here van almal!

Kroon Hom, o ogendsterre van lig,
Wat hierdie wentelende bal vasgestel het,
Hail nou die Krag van Israël se mag,
En kroon Hom, Here van almal!

Kroon Hom, o martelare van julle God,
Wat van Sy altaar roep;
Verhef die stam van Jesse se riet,
En kroon Hom, Here van almal!

Julle, saad van Israel se uitverkore ras,
Julle, wat van die val verlos is,
Hail Hom wat julle deur Sy genade red
En kroon Hom, Here van almal!

Hail Hom, erfgename van Dawid se nageslag,
Wie Dawid as Here geroep het.
Die God vlees geword, Mens goddellik,
En kroon Hom, Here van almal!

Sondares, wie se liefde nooit kan vergeet
Die erdwurg en die gal nie,
Gaan sprei julle trophies aan Sy voete uit,
En kroon Hom, Here van almal!

Laat elke stam en elke tong
Wat die geskape roep gebind het
Nou uitroep in ’n universele lied,
Die gekroonde Here van almal!

Soos dit nou in ons liedboeke staan, is die gesang verkort en verander, en een stanza is deur die beroemde liederversamelaar, ds. John Rippon, in 1787 bygevoeg.

O ja, met daardie heilige skare
Mag ons by Sy voete val;
Ons sal by die ewige lied aansluit,
En Hom kroon, Here van almal.

Terwyl ons hierdie wonderlike verhaal van Edward Perronet se lewe en van die ander wat hul deel gehad het om hierdie onsterflike gesang aan ons te bring afsluit, kom ons in afsluiting kyk na die uitwerking wat hierdie gesang op heidene gehad het wat niks van Jesus geweet het nie. Die bekendste verhaal wat met Perronet se groot gesang verbind word, word vertel van die predikant in Indië, ds. E.P. Scott. Op ’n dag het hy ’n man in die straat gesien van so vreemde voorkoms dat hy oor hom navraag gedoen en verneem het dat hy tot ’n wilde bergstam behoort waartydens Christus nog nooit verkondig is nie. Mnr. Scott het oor die saak gebid en besluit om die stam te besoek. Sodra hy hul berghuis bereik het, het hy onder ’n woeste bende moorddadige stamlede geval wat op ’n oorlogstog was en wat met hul spiesse op hom toegesluit het. Hulle het hom gegryp en hul spiesse na sy hart gerig. Dadelik het die sendeling die viool uitgehaal wat hy altyd by hom gedra het en begin speel en sing in die plaaslike taal, “All hail the power of Jesus’ name!” Hy het sy oë toegemaak en verwag om enige oomblik te sterf. Toe hy by die vierde stanza kom en niks gebeur het nie, het hy sy oë oopgemaak en was verbaas om te sien dat die spiesse uit die hande van die wredees geval het, en groot trane in hul oë was! Hulle het mnr. Scott na hul huise uitgenooi, en hy het die oorblywende jare van sy lewe daarmee bestee om hierdie mense die evangelie en God se liefde en verlossing voor te hou. God het in Sy voorsienigheid ’n eenvoudige gesang as ’n middel gebruik om die evangelie aan ’n groep behoeftige heidene bekend te stel.

At the prime age of 40, he found himself <em>…learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and was mighty in words and in deeds. And when he was full forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brethren the children of Israel –Acts 7:22-23.</em></p> <p>I have no doubt that God can, and does, use men of great ability, capacity, and training, but spiritual leadership requires an ingredient that is not derived from doing, attaining, and accomplishing. The bane of the zealot is often too little confidence in God and too much confidence in the flesh. This pride and restlessness is not dealt with in a seminary nor is it normally exterminated during vigilant duty. For many of God’s servants, it is extracted from the soul on the soil of deserted sands. This arid and abandoned acreage that appears void of life and fruitfulness is where many servants learn to put their face in the dust and yield to what may seem to be inactivity, unfruitfulness, and rejection.</p> <p>Moses’ life could be divided into three sections. He spent his first forty years learning the wisdom of Egypt, the next forty as a shepherd in Midian, and a final forty as the shepherd of Israel. We can imagine that the first third of his pilgrimage was filled with tremendous activity, advancement, and accomplishment. It had undoubtedly been rehearsed to him that at his birth he <em>…was exceeding fair, and nourished up in his father’s house three months –Acts 7:20.</em></p> <p>The miraculous river rescue by Pharoah’s daughter would serve to confirm that he was destined to be an instrument of God’s divine orchestration. As a centerpiece of national attention, it is certainly understandable how this man who <em>…was mighty in words and in deeds –Acts 7:22,</em> was brimming with self-confidence in his ability to accomplish God’s bidding.</p> <p>In today’s economy, Moses would be esteemed as the ideal candidate for church leadership. He was in every way qualified. He stood above his countrymen in education, and he possessed above-normal natural, financial, and spiritual endowments. He had emerged from the “University” of Egypt as a man mighty in word and deed and he had an obvious call from God upon his life. He was a conservative man who chose <em>…rather to suffer affliction with the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season –Hebrews 11:25.</em></p> <p>Still, amidst all his fine credentials he was yet deficient for the work that God had called him to. And so, God conveniently conducted him into the land of Midian to enroll him in another school to feed upon the bitter herbs of disappointment and rejection, obscurity and loneliness, and unfulfilled dreams and longings. While it was his earlier ambition to voluntarily align himself with the people of God, this chapter of his life was enacted by compulsion.</p> <p>We learn from the account in Exodus that the latter third of his life was loaded with intricate involvement and major ministry. While the exit from Egypt is an exciting read and provides great insight, most of us cannot honestly relate to the mighty Moses and his dynamic coalition with God. Rather, it is the uneventful 40-year mid-section of his life that many of us find ourselves in. Though there are but a few dozen verses that represent these four decades of his life, we assume that it was a thorough schooling that inscribed immense patience, soul searching, and perhaps a bit of frustration.</p> <p>For us, it represents a period when the parched sands of time about us seem to be producing nothing more fruitful than a revelation of our dry, crusty heart—shriveled and wasted by the consequences of our failures and past sins. It is at these times that we can have a lapse in faith, not that we blame God for our circumstances, but that we may begin to see our lives as futile, and that each day is the same as the previous one. Perhaps we begin to walk around in a visionless stupor—through a fog of spiritual depression—as we grope for encouragement and a reminder that God has not forgotten us. At times, it even seems that our prayers hit the ceiling and bounce back, laughing and lying to us in grim mockery that our usefulness in the Kingdom of God is over. During extended times of trials and testing, we can feel abandoned. We can even imagine that God has turned against us. We look up to Heaven and ask, “Why Lord?” We will never experience rejection and being forsaken to the extent that the Lord Jesus did, but when we experience them in our petty little realm, it seems to sap all our spiritual strength and vigor. We think… <em>If the Lord should require forty years of this from us there would be no time left in our lives to capitalize on what we have learned.</em> But God’s timing is perfect. Thus, it behooves us to not concern ourselves so much with the longevity of our schooling, but to be thoroughly acquainted with the message from Midian. While some receive the bitter strokes of Midian and retreat to stand cynically on the sidelines, we must shake off the dust of the desert and arise with an understanding of…</p> <h2>God’s Purpose</h2> <p>God has a purpose for every detail of our lives. He may plant us in a difficult position, to forge in us a new vocation. It was alone in Midian where Moses learned of his own pride, self-confidence, lack of faith, and the utter folly that his own hands had participated in. Here in his Midian, he was alone and yet not alone; numerous other saints have joined him there. The sons of Jacob and the wife of Potiphar sent another vibrant servant there—Joseph. The wild rage of a jealous king sent a gifted young harpist there. Even an old and foolish king who refused to be taught found himself in a wilderness eating grass like an ox until he recanted of his pride.</p> <p>Throughout the pages of history, countless saints have realized that ‘the darker the valley, the more I learned to pray’. While they arrive at the threshold of the new day loaded down with bountiful exuberance, they are soon stripped naked in a metamorphic change and finally emerge with nothing but the rod of God in their hands. Gone are the days when they were swift to speak, swift to act, and slow to hear. In Midian, the student learns to shift his focus from, “I will do great things for God” to “What wilt thou have me to do?”</p> <p><em>And he trembling and astonished said, Lord, what wilt thou have me to do? And the Lord said unto him, Arise, and go into the city, and it shall be told thee what thou must do –Acts 9:6.</em> The new arrivals in Midian have many answers, but most of them involve a one-act-play with self as the main character. The graduates walk out silent and sober, for they’ve come through the arduous process of separating the flesh from the spirit which was accomplished by…</p> <h2>God’s Purging</h2> <p><em>The fining pot is for silver, and the furnace for gold: but the LORD trieth the hearts –Proverbs 17:3.</em> As Moses passed through the gates of Midian, the first scene that God set before his eyes was an injustice at a well. <em>Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters… –Exodus 2:16</em>, who were being driven away by a band of uncouth shepherds. But Moses had been well trained in every dimension of Egyptian plutocracy, which would have included all aspects of military expertise and worldly leadership skills. Thus, when he stepped in to assist the helpless shepherdesses, he would have been quite capable to do so. These daughters of the priest of Midian appreciated the help which they recounted to their father that <em>…An Egyptian delivered us out of the hand of the shepherds, and also drew water enough for us, and watered the flock –Exodus 2:19.</em> Upon hearing this tale, their father, Reuel, was so impressed that he gave Moses a reception, a job, and a wife… all in one verse. <em>–see Exodus 2:21.</em></p> <p><em>…Ye know that they which are accounted to rule over the Gentiles exercise lordship over them; and their great ones exercise authority upon them –Mark 10:42.</em> While Moses’ quest for justice may have been noble, his orientation was merely Gentile. This may work for establishing pecking order in a hen house, but it is destined for failure in leading forth the people of God. <em>But … whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister: And whosoever of you will be the chiefest, shall be servant of all –Mark 10:43-44.</em></p> <p>This doctrine was foreign to Egypt and to Moses as well. Many good and talented men can successfully operate a business using Gentile authority, but it rarely works in their home, and it is even more futile in a church. Thus, God moved His chosen vessel from royalty to proletariat (the working class), almost overnight. He is then given a job which was loathed by the people who had trained him—<em>…for every shepherd is an abomination unto the Egyptians –Genesis 46:34.</em> This fining pot is not just to teach us a much-needed lesson, but to guide us into…</p> <h2>God’s Provision</h2> <p><em>The meek will he guide in judgment: and the meek will he teach his way –Psalm 25:9.</em> God will never abandon us on the back side of the desert; instead, He tailors our life circumstances to bring us into His fullness. If we resist the temptation to espouse an attitude of anger, then God will be able to teach us His ways. But to Moses, the situation presented itself such that God’s divine direction was the last thing he would suspect was happening.</p> <p>Happening…? It seemed that nothing was happening. The weeks melted into months, the months into years, and the years into decades, all the while the gifted Moses remained an underachieving shepherd. One of the hardest things that we struggle with is “waiting.” Almost every Christian will face a long time of tribulation and we are told to: <em>…think it not strange concerning the fiery trial which is to try you, as though some strange thing happened unto you –1 Peter 4:12.</em> But we should not judge God’s means by our feeble sense, for in the meantime, the wonderful working of waiting prepares us for…</p> <h2>God’s Promotion</h2> <p>38, 39, … 40 years. <em>Come <strong>now</strong> therefore, and I will send thee unto Pharaoh, that thou mayest bring forth my people the children of Israel out of Egypt –Exodus 3:10.</em></p> <p>Perhaps God is enamored with the number 40, but more than likely, it was the time that it took for Moses to land at the seat of resignation. His self-esteem has been fully extinguished, and he humbly asks: <em>…Who am I, that I should go unto Pharaoh, and that I should bring forth the children of Israel out of Egypt? –Exodus 3:11.</em></p> <p>Moses was not less qualified than he was forty years prior to this time, but his presumption had evaporated in the heat of the desert sun. The experience gleaned in the rugged pastures with the stubborn sheep has brought him to the understanding that this will be nearly an impossible feat. But there is no ordained calling issued independently from…</p> <h2>God’s Promise</h2> <p><em>…Certainly I will be with thee; and this shall be a token unto thee, that I have sent thee: When thou hast brought forth the people out of Egypt, ye shall serve God upon this mountain –Exodus 3:12.</em></p> <p>Not that Moses had attained perfection, for we find Moses provoking God to anger in the very next chapter—<em>And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Moses… –Exodus 4:14.</em> Then soon again he is the direct object in the path of God’s sword—<em>And it came to pass by the way in the inn, that the LORD met him, and sought to kill him –Exodus 4:24.</em> Even so, while his vessel is still made of clay, it has met with a firing that has prepared him for the Lord’s service, and for us God will not revoke His promises in the wind of our whims. Thus, the great I AM THAT I AM <em>–see Exodus 3:14</em>, has laid upon human shoulders the immense and eternal task of leading His people. But this charge is not to be executed without…</p> <h2>God’s Power</h2> <p>What was the real refinement from Moses’ time spent in the desert? We notice his rash willingness to wield the sword before his arrival, but upon his exit, he only bore a rod in his hand. With the sword he had overcome an Egyptian offender, but with the rod he overcame the entire forces of Egypt. The rod of God brought forth the water in the wilderness. It was the rod of God, that, when lifted high by feeble hands secured the victory over Amalek. What is the rod of God? Before his days in Midian, he hardly knew it existed. Forty years later there hardly exists a scene without it.</p> <p>The rod is the power of God unto salvation. It is the wisdom of God, the truth of God, the testimony of God, but more than all of these it is the chastening of God. Without it, man does not receive nor perceive the love of God for without it man is not connected to God. <em>For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth. If ye endure chastening, God dealeth with you as with sons; for what son is he whom the father chasteneth not? But if ye be without chastisement, whereof all are partakers, then are ye bastards, and not sons –Hebrews 12:6-8.</em></p> <p>This same Moses, who at one time was willing to exercise lordship (Gentile authority) over God’s people now finds himself entreating God and staying His wrath from destroying them. The people who accused Moses of leading them out to kill them and even at one point were ready to stone him are now at the center of his heart and affection, even though they are at the cause of his failure to enter the promised land. This is the love of Christ. But where is this learned except under the rod of God, on the back side of the desert, in the Egyptian dungeons, in the caves of Adullam, in the straits of Arabia, and in the silent solitude of the back burner where God has ordained that many of His people go until they learn to <em>…learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls –Matthew 11:29.</em> Surely that is where Moses secured the character known to the biblical scholar as the meekest man to walk the face of the earth. Surely there is no more opposite place on earth to learn it but in the school of suffering.</p> <p>And so here we shall abide as well, so that we <em>…may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, being made conformable unto his death –Philippians 3:10.</em></p> <figure> <img src="/images/articles/53e8b534-1f5e-4d9d-b191-99707a404256-1.jpg" alt="A broad desert valley beneath layered mountains and clouds" loading="lazy"> </figure> </article> ","section":"CHARACTER STUDIES","subtitle":null,"title":"Moses in Midian"},"source_context":{"byline":{"authors":[{"location":"Athens, WI","name":"Lee Rufener"}],"raw":"by Lee Rufener Athens, WI"}},"target_language":"Italian","terminology_glossary":{},"translation":{"html":"<article data-article-id="53e8b534-1f5e-4d9d-b191-99707a404256"> <p><em>Ora Mosè pascolava il gregge di Ietro, suo suocero, sacerdote di Madian; e condusse il gregge dietro il deserto, e venne al monte di Dio, a Horeb –Esodo 3:1.</em></p> <p>Il retro del deserto è da tempo inteso come la scuola di Dio nella quale Egli ha istruito molti dei suoi servi, di cui Mosè è il principale. All’età matura di 40 anni, si trovò <em>…istruito di tutta la sapienza degli Egiziani, ed era potente nelle parole e nelle opere. E quando ebbe compiuto quaranta anni, gli venne in cuore di visitare i suoi fratelli, i figli d’Israele –Atti 7:22-23.</em></p> <p>Non ho dubbio che Dio possa, e usi, uomini di grande abilità, capacità e formazione, ma la leadership spirituale richiede un ingrediente che non deriva dal fare, conseguire e compiere. Il male dello zelante è spesso avere troppo poca fiducia in Dio e troppa fiducia nella carne. Questo orgoglio e questa irrequietezza non si affrontano in un seminario né normalmente si estirpano durante il servizio vigile. Per molti servi di Dio, esso viene estratto dall’anima nel suolo delle sabbie deserte. Questa terra arida e abbandonata che appare priva di vita e di frutto è dove molti servitori imparano a mettere il volto nella polvere e a cedere a ciò che può sembrare inattività, infertilità e rifiuto.</p> <p>La vita di Mosè può essere divisa in tre sezioni. Trascorse i suoi primi quaranta anni apprendendo la sapienza dell’Egitto, i successivi quaranta come pastore in Madian, e gli ultimi quaranta come pastore d’Israele. Possiamo immaginare che il primo terzo del suo pellegrinaggio fosse pieno di grande attività, avanzamento e realizzazione. Gli era senza dubbio stato ripetuto che alla sua nascita egli <em>…era bellissimo, e fu nutrito nella casa di suo padre tre mesi –Atti 7:20.</em></p> <p>Il miracoloso salvataggio nel fiume da parte della figlia del faraone servì a confermare che era destinato a essere uno strumento dell’orchestrazione divina di Dio. Come centro dell’attenzione nazionale, è certamente comprensibile come quest’uomo che <em>…era potente nelle parole e nelle opere –Atti 7:22,</em> fosse colmo di fiducia in sé nella sua capacità di adempiere il volere di Dio.</p> <p>Nell’economia odierna, Mosè sarebbe considerato il candidato ideale per la leadership di chiesa. Era sotto ogni aspetto qualificato. Si distingueva tra i suoi connazionali per l’istruzione, e possedeva doni naturali, finanziari e spirituali sopra la norma. Era uscito dall’“Università” d’Egitto come un uomo potente nella parola e nell’opera e aveva una chiamata evidente di Dio sulla sua vita. Era un uomo conservatore che scelse <em>…piuttosto di soffrire afflizione col popolo di Dio, che godere dei piaceri del peccato per un poco –Ebrei 11:25.</em></p> <p>Tuttavia, in mezzo a tutti i suoi ottimi titoli era ancora carente per l’opera a cui Dio lo aveva chiamato. E così, Dio convenientemente lo condusse nella terra di Madian per iscriverlo in un’altra scuola dove nutrirsi delle amare erbe della delusione e del rifiuto, dell’oscurità e della solitudine, e dei sogni e desideri non realizzati. Mentre prima era sua ambizione allinearsi volontariamente col popolo di Dio, questo capitolo della sua vita si svolse per costrizione.</p> <p>Apprendiamo dal racconto in Esodo che l’ultimo terzo della sua vita fu carico di coinvolgimenti intricati e di ministero rilevante. Sebbene l’uscita dall’Egitto sia una lettura eccitante e fornisca grande intuizione, la maggior parte di noi non può onestamente relazionarsi con il possente Mosè e la sua coalizione dinamica con Dio. Piuttosto, è la monotona sezione mediana di 40 anni della sua vita in cui molti di noi si ritrovano. Sebbene vi siano solo poche dozzine di versetti che rappresentano questi quattro decenni della sua vita, supponiamo che sia stata un’istruzione approfondita che ha inciso immensa pazienza, ricerca dell’anima, e forse un po’ di frustrazione.</p> <p>Per noi rappresenta un periodo in cui le sabbie aride del tempo intorno a noi sembrano produrre nient’altro che la rivelazione del nostro cuore secco e crostoso—avvizzito e sprecato dalle conseguenze dei nostri fallimenti e peccati passati. È in questi momenti che possiamo avere una battuta d’arresto nella fede, non perché biasimiamo Dio per le nostre circostanze, ma perché possiamo iniziare a vedere le nostre vite come inutili, e che ogni giorno è uguale al precedente. Forse cominciamo a camminare in uno stordimento senza visione—attraverso una nebbia di depressione spirituale—mentre brancoliamo per un incoraggiamento e un promemoria che Dio non ci ha dimenticati. A volte, sembra persino che le nostre preghiere urtino il soffitto e rimbalzino indietro, ridendo e mentendo a noi in cupo scherno che la nostra utilità nel Regno di Dio è finita. Durante lunghi periodi di prove e tentazioni, possiamo sentirci abbandonati. Possiamo persino immaginare che Dio si sia rivoltato contro di noi. Alziamo lo sguardo al Cielo e chiediamo: “Perché, Signore?” Non sperimenteremo mai il rifiuto e l’essere abbandonati nella misura in cui li sperimentò il Signore Gesù, ma quando li sperimentiamo nel nostro piccolo regno, sembra prosciugare tutta la nostra forza e vigore spirituale. Pensiamo… <em>Se il Signore dovesse richiederci quaranta anni di questo non rimarrebbe tempo nelle nostre vite per capitalizzare ciò che abbiamo imparato.</em> Ma il tempo di Dio è perfetto. Pertanto, ci conviene non preoccuparci tanto della durata della nostra scuola, ma di essere completamente familiari col messaggio di Madian. Mentre alcuni ricevono i colpi amari di Madian e si ritirano per stare cinicamente ai margini, dobbiamo scrollarci di dosso la polvere del deserto e sorgere con una comprensione di…</p> <h2>Il proposito di Dio</h2> <p>Dio ha uno scopo per ogni dettaglio delle nostre vite. Egli può piantarci in una posizione difficile, per forgiare in noi una nuova vocazione. Fu solo in Madian che Mosè apprese del proprio orgoglio, fiducia in sé, mancanza di fede, e della totale follia a cui le sue mani avevano partecipato. Qui, nel suo Madian, era solo e tuttavia non solo; numerosi altri santi lo hanno raggiunto lì. I figli di Giacobbe e la moglie di Potifar mandarono un altro servo vibrante lì—Giuseppe. La furia selvaggia di un re geloso mandò lì un giovane arpaista dotato. Persino un re vecchio e sciocco che rifiutò di essere ammaestrato si trovò in una desolazione a mangiare erba come un bue finché non rinunciò al suo orgoglio.</p> <p>Attraverso le pagine della storia, innumerevoli santi hanno realizzato che «più oscura è la valle, più imparo a pregare». Pur arrivando alla soglia del nuovo giorno carichi di esuberanza, sono presto denudati in un cambiamento metamorfico e infine emergono con nient’altro che il bastone di Dio nelle mani. Sono spariti i giorni in cui erano pronti a parlare, pronti ad agire e lenti ad ascoltare. In Madian, lo studente impara a spostare il suo focus da “Farò grandi cose per Dio” a “Che vuoi che io faccia?”</p> <p><em>E quello tremando e stupefatto disse: Signore, che vuoi che io faccia? E il Signore gli disse: Alzati e va nella città, e sarà detto a te ciò che devi fare –Atti 9:6.</em> I nuovi arrivati a Madian hanno molte risposte, ma la maggior parte di esse riguardano una pièce in un atto con il sé come personaggio principale. I diplomati escono silenziosi e sobri, poiché sono passati attraverso l’arduo processo di separare la carne dallo spirito che fu compiuto da…</p> <h2>La purificazione di Dio</h2> <p><em>Il crogiuolo è per l’argento, e il forno per l’oro; ma il Signore mette alla prova i cuori –Proverbi 17:3.</em> Quando Mosè varcò i cancelli di Madian, la prima scena che Dio pose davanti ai suoi occhi fu un’ingiustizia a un pozzo. <em>Ora il sacerdote di Madian aveva sette figlie… –Esodo 2:16</em>, che venivano respinte da una banda di pastori rozzi. Ma Mosè era stato ben istruito in ogni dimensione della plutocrazia egiziana, che avrebbe incluso tutti gli aspetti dell’esperienza militare e delle abilità di leadership mondane. Così, quando intervenne per aiutare le pastorelle indifese, sarebbe stato più che capace di farlo. Queste figlie del sacerdote di Madian apprezzarono l’aiuto al punto che lo riferirono al padre dicendo che <em>…Un Egiziano ci liberò dalla mano dei pastori, e anche attingeva acqua per noi, e diede da bere al gregge –Esodo 2:19.</em> Sentendo questo racconto, il loro padre, Reuel, fu così impressionato che diede a Mosè un’accoglienza, un lavoro e una moglie… il tutto in un verso. <em>–vedi Esodo 2:21.</em></p> <p><em>…Sapete che quelli che sono considerati governare sulle nazioni le dominano; e i loro grandi esercitano potere su di esse –Marco 10:42.</em> Sebbene la ricerca di giustizia di Mosè potesse essere nobile, la sua orientazione era puramente gentile. Questo può funzionare per stabilire l’ordine di supremazia in un pollaio, ma è destinato al fallimento nel condurre il popolo di Dio. <em>Ma… chi vorrà essere grande fra voi, sarà vostro servitore; e chi fra voi sarà il primo, sarà il servo di tutti –Marco 10:43-44.</em></p> <p>Questa dottrina era straniera all’Egitto e anche a Mosè. Molti uomini buoni e talentuosi possono gestire con successo un’impresa usando l’autorità gentile, ma raramente funziona nella loro casa, ed è ancor più inutile in una chiesa. Così, Dio spostò il suo vaso scelto dalla regalità al proletariato (la classe lavoratrice), quasi da un giorno all’altro. Gli fu quindi dato un lavoro disprezzato dalle persone che lo avevano formato—<em>…poiché ogni pastore è abominevole agli Egiziani –Genesi 46:34.</em> Questo crogiuolo non è solo per insegnarci una lezione tanto necessaria, ma per guidarci verso…</p> <h2>La provvidenza di Dio</h2> <p><em>I mansueti egli li guida nel giudizio; egli insegna la sua via agli umili –Salmi 25:9.</em> Dio non ci abbandonerà mai sul retro del deserto; invece, modella le nostre circostanze di vita per portarci nella sua pienezza. Se resistiamo alla tentazione di assumere un atteggiamento di rabbia, allora Dio sarà in grado di insegnarci le sue vie. Ma per Mosè la situazione si presentò in modo che la direzione divina di Dio fosse l’ultima cosa che avrebbe sospettato stesse accadendo.</p> <p>Che stesse accadendo…? Sembrava che nulla stesse accadendo. Le settimane si scioglievano in mesi, i mesi in anni, e gli anni in decenni, mentre il dotato Mosè rimaneva un pastore sotto rendimento. Una delle cose più difficili con cui lottiamo è «aspettare». Quasi ogni cristiano affronterà un lungo tempo di tribolazione e ci è detto di: <em>…non pensate strano della prova di fuoco che è per provare voi, come se vi fosse cosa strana che vi accadesse –1 Pietro 4:12.</em> Ma non dovremmo giudicare i mezzi di Dio dal nostro fiacco senso, perché nel frattempo lo meraviglioso operare dell’attesa ci prepara per…</p> <h2>La promozione di Dio</h2> <p>38, 39, … 40 anni. <em>Vieni <strong>ora</strong> dunque, e io ti manderò da Faraone, affinché tu faccia uscire il mio popolo, i figli d’Israele, dall’Egitto –Esodo 3:10.</em></p> <p>Forse a Dio piace il numero 40, ma molto più probabilmente fu il tempo che servì a far cadere Mosè nel luogo della rinuncia. La sua autostima era stata completamente spenta, e umilmente chiede: <em>…Chi sono io, perché io vada da Faraone, e perché io faccia uscire i figli d’Israele dall’Egitto? –Esodo 3:11.</em></p> <p>Mosè non era meno qualificato di quanto fosse quarant’anni prima, ma la sua presunzione era evaporata nel calore del sole del deserto. L’esperienza acquisita nei pascoli aspri con le pecore testarde lo aveva portato a comprendere che ciò sarebbe stato quasi un’impresa impossibile. Ma non esiste chiamata ordinata che sia emessa indipendentemente da…</p> <h2>La promessa di Dio</h2> <p><em>…Certo io sarò con te; e questa ti sarà per segno che io ti ho mandato: Quando avrai fatto uscire il popolo dall’Egitto, servirete Dio su questo monte –Esodo 3:12.</em></p> <p>Non che Mosè avesse raggiunto la perfezione, poiché troviamo Mosè a irritare Dio nell’immediato capitolo successivo—<em>E l’ira del Signore si accese contro Mosè… –Esodo 4:14.</em> Poi di nuovo egli è oggetto diretto nel cammino della spada di Dio—<em>E avvenne per la via nell’albergo, che il Signore lo incontrò e volle farlo morire –Esodo 4:24.</em> Nonostante ciò, mentre il suo vaso è ancora di argilla, ha subito una cottura che lo ha preparato per il servizio del Signore, e per noi Dio non revoca le sue promesse al vento dei nostri capricci. Dunque, il grande IO SONO COLUI CHE SONO <em>–vedi Esodo 3:14</em>, ha posto sulle spalle umane l’immensa e eterna impresa di guidare il suo popolo. Ma questo incarico non deve essere eseguito senza…</p> <h2>La potenza di Dio</h2> <p>Qual è stata la vera raffinazione del tempo che Mosè trascorse nel deserto? Notiamo la sua pronta inclinazione a brandire la spada prima del suo arrivo, ma al suo uscire portava solo un bastone in mano. Con la spada aveva vinto un offender Egiziano, ma con il bastone sconfisse le forze intere d’Egitto. Il bastone di Dio fece sgorgare acqua nel deserto. Fu il bastone di Dio che, quando elevato in alto da mani fragili, assicurò la vittoria su Amalek. Cos’è il bastone di Dio? Prima dei suoi giorni in Madian, a malapena ne conosceva l’esistenza. Quarant’anni dopo quasi non esiste scena senza di esso.</p> <p>Il bastone è la potenza di Dio per la salvezza. È la sapienza di Dio, la verità di Dio, la testimonianza di Dio, ma più di tutte queste è la castigazione di Dio. Senza di esso, l’uomo non riceve né percepisce l’amore di Dio perché senza di esso l’uomo non è connesso a Dio. <em>Perché il Signore corregge chi ama, e castiga ogni figlio che riceve. Se sopportate la correzione, Dio vi tratta come figli; poiché qual figlio è quello che il padre non corregge? Ma se siete senza correzione, della quale tutti sono partecipi, siete bastardi e non figli –Ebrei 12:6-8.</em></p> <p>Quello stesso Mosè, che un tempo era disposto ad esercitare signoria (autorità gentile) sul popolo di Dio ora si trova a supplicare Dio e a trattenere la sua ira dall’anneggiarli. Le persone che accusarono Mosè di condurli fuori per farli morire e che a un certo punto erano pronte a lapidarlo sono ora al centro del suo cuore e della sua affezione, sebbene siano causa del suo fallimento nell’entrare nella terra promessa. Questo è l’amore di Cristo. Ma dove si apprende questo se non sotto il bastone di Dio, sul retro del deserto, nelle segrete egiziane, nelle caverne di Adulàm, nelle ristrettezze dell’Arabia, e nella silenziosa solitudine del retro fuoco dove Dio ha ordinato che molti dei suoi vadano finché imparino a <em>…imparare da me; perché io sono mansueto e umile di cuore: e troverete riposo alle vostre anime –Matteo 11:29.</em> Sicuramente è lì che Mosè assicurò il carattere noto allo studioso biblico come l’uomo più mansueto che abbia camminato sulla faccia della terra. Sicuramente non c’è luogo più opposto sulla terra per impararlo se non nella scuola della sofferenza.</p> <p>E così qui dimoreremo anche noi, affinché <em>…possiamo conoscerlo, e la potenza della sua risurrezione, e la comunione delle sue sofferenze, essendo fatti conformi alla sua morte –Filippesi 3:10.</em></p> <figure> <img src="/images/articles/53e8b534-1f5e-4d9d-b191-99707a404256-1.jpg" alt="Una ampia valle desertica sotto montagne stratificate e nuvole" loading="lazy"> </figure> </article> ","section":"CHARACTER STUDIES","subtitle":null,"title":"Moses in Midian"}}

Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honour and power: for thou hast created all things, and for thy pleasure they are and were created –Revelation 4:11.

This hymn, often called the “National Anthem of Christendom,” is perhaps one of the greatest of hymns of all time. It was written by Edward Perronet, first appearing in the November 1779 issue of Gospel Magazine. It was edited by Augustus Toplady, who is also the author of another well-known hymn, “Rock of Ages”. The text of this hymn, All Hail the Power of Jesus Name, has been translated into almost every language where Christianity is known. Wherever it is sung, it communicates to the spiritual needs of human hearts. One writer has said, “So long as there are Christians on earth, it will continue to be sung; and after that, in heaven.”

Edward Perronet was born at Sundridge, Kent, England, in 1726. He was a descendant of a distinguished French Huguenot family who had fled to Switzerland and later to England because of the religious persecution in France. Edward’s father, a pastor in the State Church of England, was strongly sympathetic with the evangelical movement spearheaded by the Wesleys and George Whitefield. Edward, too, like his father, became a minister in the Anglican Church but was always critical of its ways. Once he wrote, “I was born and I am likely to die in the tottering communion of the Church of England, but I despise her nonsense.” Soon, however, he broke from the Church and threw himself strenuously into the evangelistic endeavors of the Wesleys during the 1740s and 1750s.

Charles Wesley writes of Edward Perronet’s boldness in preaching. At one time he and Perronet were beset in a house by a mob of rough revilers, whom Perronet opposed courageously, while they abused him and threw dirt on him. It was during this time that the Wesleys and their followers suffered much persecution and even violence from those who disagreed with their ministry. Concerning these experiences, Wesley made the following notation in his diary: “From Rockdale we went to Bolton, and soon found that the Rockdale lions were lambs in comparison with those of Bolton.” Edward Perronet was thrown down and rolled in mud and mire. Stones were hurled and windows broken.

Another interesting account is given regarding the relationship between the Wesleys and Perronet. John Wesley wanted to hear Perronet preach, and he, being 18 years younger than John had always refused to preach in the older churchman’s presence. So, one day Wesley seeing Edward in the congregation announced that he would preach at the next service. Desiring to avoid a public conflict with Wesley, Perronet mounted the pulpit the next morning, but quickly explained that he had never consented to preach. “However,” he added, “I shall deliver the greatest sermon that has ever been preached on earth.” He then read the Sermon on the Mount and sat down without comment.

After eight years of co-operation with the Wesleys, Perronet’s strong-mindedness and free spirit caused a division between them, as he disagreed with some of their regulations. They continued, however, to esteem and love each other.

The last years of Perronet were spent at Canterbury, where he was pastor of an independent church, and where he died in 1792, at the age of sixty-six. His last words have also become a classic: “Glory to God in the height of His divinity! Glory to God in the depth of His humanity! Glory to God in His all-sufficiency! Into His hands I commend my spirit.”

Though Perronet wrote many other hymns and forms of poetry, none of them, have attained fame except the immortal “All Hail the Power of Jesus Name.” The success of this text has, no doubt, been furthered by three fine tunes. “Coronation,” composed by Oliver Holden, a Massachusetts carpenter, self-taught musician, and respected singing-school teacher, is most widely used in America. “Miles Lane” composed by William Shrubsole, Perronet’s personal friend, is the most popular in Great Britain. While the festive “Diadem” tune, composed in 1838 for this text by James Ellor, an English layman, is frequently used as a choir number. This hymn was originally written having the title, “On the Resurrection,” and there were eight stanzas, as follows:

All hail the power of Jesus’ name,
Let angels prostrate fall
Bring forth the royal diadem,
To crown Him Lord of all!

Let high born seraphs tune the lyre,
And, as they tune it, fall
Before His face who tunes their choir,
And crown Him Lord of all!

Crown Him, ye morning stars of light,
Who fixed this floating ball,
Now hail the Strength of Israel’s might,
And crown Him Lord of all!

Crown Him, ye martyrs of your God,
Who from His altar call;
Extol the stem of Jesse’s rod,
And crown Him Lord of all!

Ye seed of Israel’s chosen race,
Ye ransomed of the fall,
Hail Him who saves you by His grace
And crown Him Lord of all!

Hail Him, ye heirs of David’s line,
Whom David Lord did call.
The God incarnate, Man divine,
And crown Him Lord of all!

Sinners, whose love can ne’er forget
The wormwood and the gall,
Go spread your trophies at His feet,
And crown Him Lord of all!

Let every tribe and every tongue
That bound creation’s call
Now shout in universal song,
The crowned Lord of all!

As it now stands in our hymnbooks, the hymn is shortened and changed, and one stanza has been added by the famous hymn collector, Rev. John Rippon, in 1787.

Oh, that with yonder sacred throng
We at His feet may fall;
We’ll join the everlasting song,
And crown Him Lord of all.

As we wrap up this amazing story of the life of Edward Perronet and the others who have had their part in bringing this immortal hymn to us, let’s take a look in closing at the effect this hymn has had on heathens who knew nothing about Jesus. The most famous story connected with Perronet’s great hymn is told of the missionary to India, Rev. E.P. Scott. One day he saw on the street a man of so strange an appearance that he inquired about him and learned that he belonged to a wild mountain tribe among whom Christ had never been preached. Mr. Scott prayed over the matter and decided to visit that tribe. As soon as he reached their mountain home, he fell in among a savage band of murderous tribesmen who were on a war expedition, and who were closing in on him with their spears. They seized him and pointed their spears at his heart. At once the missionary drew out the violin that he always carried with him and began to play and sing in the native language, “All hail the power of Jesus’ name!” He closed his eyes, expecting death at any minute. When he reached the fourth stanza, and nothing had happened, he opened his eyes, and was amazed to see that the spears had fallen from the hands of the savages, and big tears were in their eyes! They invited Mr. Scott to their homes, and he spent the remaining years of his life preaching and ministering God’s love and redemption to these people. God in His providence used a simple hymn as a means of introducing the gospel to a group of needy pagans.

Tu es digne, ô Seigneur, de recevoir la gloire, l'honneur et la puissance: car tu as créé toutes choses, et c'est pour ton plaisir qu'elles existent et ont été créées –Apocalypse 4:11.

Cet hymne, souvent appelé «l'hymne national du christianisme», est peut-être l'un des plus grands hymnes de tous les temps. Il a été écrit par Edward Perronet et est paru pour la première fois dans le numéro de novembre 1779 du Gospel Magazine. Il a été édité par Augustus Toplady, qui est aussi l'auteur d'un autre hymne bien connu, «Rock of Ages». Le texte de cet hymne, All Hail the Power of Jesus Name, a été traduit dans presque toutes les langues où le christianisme est connu. Partout où il est chanté, il répond aux besoins spirituels des cœurs humains. Un écrivain a dit : «Tant qu'il y aura des chrétiens sur terre, il continuera d'être chanté; et ensuite, au ciel.»

Edward Perronet est né à Sundridge, dans le Kent, en Angleterre, en 1726. Il descendait d'une illustre famille huguenote française qui avait fui en Suisse puis en Angleterre à cause des persécutions religieuses en France. Le père d'Edward, pasteur dans l'Église d'Angleterre, était fortement sympathisant du mouvement évangélique mené par les frères Wesley et George Whitefield. Edward, lui aussi, comme son père, devint ministre dans l'Église anglicane mais fut toujours critique à l'égard de ses façons. Il écrivit une fois : «Je suis né et je suis susceptible de mourir dans la communion vacillante de l'Église d'Angleterre, mais je méprise ses absurdités.» Bientôt cependant, il rompit avec l'Église et se lança avec énergie dans les œuvres évangéliques des Wesley durant les années 1740 et 1750.

Charles Wesley écrit sur l'audace d'Edward Perronet dans la prédication. À une époque, lui et Perronet furent assiégés dans une maison par une foule de grossiers vociférateurs, que Perronet affronta courageusement, tandis qu'ils l'insultaient et lui jetaient de la terre. C'est à cette période que les Wesley et leurs partisans subirent beaucoup de persécution et même de la violence de la part de ceux qui désapprouvaient leur ministère. Concernant ces expériences, Wesley nota dans son journal : «De Rockdale nous sommes allés à Bolton, et nous avons bientôt trouvé que les lions de Rockdale étaient des agneaux comparés à ceux de Bolton.» Edward Perronet fut jeté à terre et roulé dans la boue et la fange. Des pierres furent lancées et des fenêtres brisées.

Un autre récit intéressant est donné concernant la relation entre les Wesley et Perronet. John Wesley désirait entendre Perronet prêcher, et lui, étant de dix-huit ans plus jeune que John, avait toujours refusé de prêcher en présence du vieux pasteur. Ainsi, un jour, Wesley voyant Edward dans la congrégation annonça qu'il prêcherait au service suivant. Désirant éviter un conflit public avec Wesley, Perronet monta en chaire le lendemain matin, mais expliqua rapidement qu'il n'avait jamais consenti à prêcher. «Cependant,» ajouta-t-il, «je livrerai le plus grand sermon qui ait jamais été prêché sur la terre.» Il lut alors le Sermon sur la montagne et s'assit sans commentaire.

Après huit années de coopération avec les Wesley, l'entêtement et l'esprit libre de Perronet provoquèrent une division entre eux, car il était en désaccord avec certaines de leurs règlements. Ils continuèrent néanmoins à s'estimer et à s'aimer.

Les dernières années de Perronet se passèrent à Canterbury, où il fut pasteur d'une église indépendante, et où il mourut en 1792, à l'âge de soixante-six ans. Ses dernières paroles sont également devenues un classique : «Gloire à Dieu dans la hauteur de Sa divinité! Gloire à Dieu dans la profondeur de Son humanité! Gloire à Dieu dans Sa suffisance totale! Entre Ses mains je recommande mon esprit.»

Bien que Perronet ait écrit de nombreux autres hymnes et poèmes, aucun d'eux n'a acquis de renommée excepté l'immortel «All Hail the Power of Jesus' Name». Le succès de ce texte a sans doute été favorisé par trois beaux airs. «Coronation», composé par Oliver Holden, un charpentier du Massachusetts, musicien autodidacte et respecté professeur d'école de chant, est le plus largement utilisé en Amérique. «Miles Lane», composé par William Shrubsole, ami personnel de Perronet, est le plus populaire en Grande-Bretagne. Tandis que l'air festif «Diadem», composé en 1838 pour ce texte par James Ellor, un laïc anglais, est fréquemment utilisé comme pièce de chœur. Cet hymne a été à l'origine écrit sous le titre «On the Resurrection», et il y avait huit strophes, comme suit :

Salut au pouvoir du nom de Jésus,
Que les anges se prosternent et tombent!
Apportez la diadème royal,
Pour le couronner Seigneur de tout!

Que les séraphins nés en haut accordent la lyre,
Et, tandis qu'ils l'accordent, s'inclinent,
Devant Sa face qui règle leur chœur,
Et le couronner Seigneur de tout!

Couronnez-Le, ô étoiles matinales de lumière,
Qui avez fixé cette boule flottante,
Saluez maintenant la Force de la puissance d'Israël,
Et couronnez-Le Seigneur de tout!

Couronnez-Le, ô martyrs de votre Dieu,
Qui l'appelez de son autel;
Exaltez la tige du bâton de Jessé,
Et couronnez-Le Seigneur de tout!

Vous, semence de la race choisie d'Israël,
Vous, rachetés de la chute,
Saluez Celui qui vous sauve par Sa grâce
Et couronnez-Le Seigneur de tout!

Saluez-Le, héritiers de la lignée de David,
Que David appelait Seigneur.
Le Dieu incarné, l'Homme divin,
Et couronnez-Le Seigneur de tout!

Pécheurs, dont l'amour ne peut jamais oublier
L'absinthe et la bile,
Allez répandre vos trophées à Ses pieds,
Et couronnez-Le Seigneur de tout!

Que chaque tribu et chaque langue
Qui a lié l'appel de la création
Crie maintenant dans un chant universel,
Le Seigneur couronné de tout!

Tel qu'il figure maintenant dans nos recueils d'hymnes, l'hymne est abrégé et modifié, et une strophe a été ajoutée par le célèbre collecteur d'hymnes, le révérend John Rippon, en 1787.

Oh, que nous, avec cette sainte multitude là-bas,
Puissions tomber à Ses pieds;
Nous nous joindrons au chant éternel,
Et le couronnerons Seigneur de tout.

Alors que nous concluons cette histoire étonnante de la vie d'Edward Perronet et des autres qui ont contribué à nous transmettre cet hymne immortel, examinons enfin l'effet qu'a eu cet hymne sur des païens qui ne connaissaient rien de Jésus. L'histoire la plus célèbre liée au grand hymne de Perronet est racontée au sujet du missionnaire en Inde, le rév. E. P. Scott. Un jour il vit dans la rue un homme d'apparence si étrange qu'il s'enquit à son sujet et apprit qu'il appartenait à une tribu montagnarde sauvage parmi laquelle le Christ n'avait jamais été prêché. M. Scott pria sur la question et décida de visiter cette tribu. Dès qu'il atteignit leur demeure montagneuse, il tomba au milieu d'une bande sauvage de tribus meurtrières qui étaient en expédition de guerre, et qui l'entouraient avec leurs lances. Ils le saisirent et pointèrent leurs lances vers son cœur. Aussitôt le missionnaire sortit le violon qu'il portait toujours avec lui et se mit à jouer et chanter dans la langue native, «All hail the power of Jesus' name!» Il ferma les yeux, s'attendant à la mort à tout instant. Lorsqu'il atteignit la quatrième strophe, et que rien ne se fut produit, il ouvrit les yeux, et fut étonné de voir que les lances étaient tombées des mains des sauvages, et de grosses larmes brillaient dans leurs yeux! Ils invitèrent M. Scott dans leurs foyers, et il passa les années restantes de sa vie à prêcher et à manifester l'amour et la rédemption de Dieu à ces peuples. Dieu, dans Sa providence, utilisa un simple hymne comme moyen d'introduire l'Évangile à un groupe de païens dans le besoin.

«Miles Lane» Tune -William Shrubsole, 1760-1806
«Diadem» Tune -James Elliot, 1838
«Let Us Crown Him» Tune -James McGranahan 1840-1907

Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honour and power: for thou hast created all things, and for thy pleasure they are and were created –Revelation 4:11.

This hymn, often called the “National Anthem of Christendom,” is perhaps one of the greatest of hymns of all time. It was written by Edward Perronet, first appearing in the November 1779 issue of Gospel Magazine. It was edited by Augustus Toplady, who is also the author of another well-known hymn, “Rock of Ages”. The text of this hymn, All Hail the Power of Jesus Name, has been translated into almost every language where Christianity is known. Wherever it is sung, it communicates to the spiritual needs of human hearts. One writer has said, “So long as there are Christians on earth, it will continue to be sung; and after that, in heaven.”

Edward Perronet was born at Sundridge, Kent, England, in 1726. He was a descendant of a distinguished French Huguenot family who had fled to Switzerland and later to England because of the religious persecution in France. Edward’s father, a pastor in the State Church of England, was strongly sympathetic with the evangelical movement spearheaded by the Wesleys and George Whitefield. Edward, too, like his father, became a minister in the Anglican Church but was always critical of its ways. Once he wrote, “I was born and I am likely to die in the tottering communion of the Church of England, but I despise her nonsense.” Soon, however, he broke from the Church and threw himself strenuously into the evangelistic endeavors of the Wesleys during the 1740s and 1750s.

Charles Wesley writes of Edward Perronet’s boldness in preaching. At one time he and Perronet were beset in a house by a mob of rough revilers, whom Perronet opposed courageously, while they abused him and threw dirt on him. It was during this time that the Wesleys and their followers suffered much persecution and even violence from those who disagreed with their ministry. Concerning these experiences, Wesley made the following notation in his diary: “From Rockdale we went to Bolton, and soon found that the Rockdale lions were lambs in comparison with those of Bolton.” Edward Perronet was thrown down and rolled in mud and mire. Stones were hurled and windows broken.

Another interesting account is given regarding the relationship between the Wesleys and Perronet. John Wesley wanted to hear Perronet preach, and he, being 18 years younger than John had always refused to preach in the older churchman’s presence. So, one day Wesley seeing Edward in the congregation announced that he would preach at the next service. Desiring to avoid a public conflict with Wesley, Perronet mounted the pulpit the next morning, but quickly explained that he had never consented to preach. “However,” he added, “I shall deliver the greatest sermon that has ever been preached on earth.” He then read the Sermon on the Mount and sat down without comment.

After eight years of co-operation with the Wesleys, Perronet’s strong-mindedness and free spirit caused a division between them, as he disagreed with some of their regulations. They continued, however, to esteem and love each other.

The last years of Perronet were spent at Canterbury, where he was pastor of an independent church, and where he died in 1792, at the age of sixty-six. His last words have also become a classic: “Glory to God in the height of His divinity! Glory to God in the depth of His humanity! Glory to God in His all-sufficiency! Into His hands I commend my spirit.”

Though Perronet wrote many other hymns and forms of poetry, none of them, have attained fame except the immortal “All Hail the Power of Jesus Name.” The success of this text has, no doubt, been furthered by three fine tunes. “Coronation,” composed by Oliver Holden, a Massachusetts carpenter, self-taught musician, and respected singing-school teacher, is most widely used in America. “Miles Lane” composed by William Shrubsole, Perronet’s personal friend, is the most popular in Great Britain. While the festive “Diadem” tune, composed in 1838 for this text by James Ellor, an English layman, is frequently used as a choir number. This hymn was originally written having the title, “On the Resurrection,” and there were eight stanzas, as follows:

All hail the power of Jesus’ name,
Let angels prostrate fall
Bring forth the royal diadem,
To crown Him Lord of all!

Let high born seraphs tune the lyre,
And, as they tune it, fall
Before His face who tunes their choir,
And crown Him Lord of all!

Crown Him, ye morning stars of light,
Who fixed this floating ball,
Now hail the Strength of Israel’s might,
And crown Him Lord of all!

Crown Him, ye martyrs of your God,
Who from His altar call;
Extol the stem of Jesse’s rod,
And crown Him Lord of all!

Ye seed of Israel’s chosen race,
Ye ransomed of the fall,
Hail Him who saves you by His grace
And crown Him Lord of all!

Hail Him, ye heirs of David’s line,
Whom David Lord did call.
The God incarnate, Man divine,
And crown Him Lord of all!

Sinners, whose love can ne’er forget
The wormwood and the gall,
Go spread your trophies at His feet,
And crown Him Lord of all!

Let every tribe and every tongue
That bound creation’s call
Now shout in universal song,
The crowned Lord of all!

As it now stands in our hymnbooks, the hymn is shortened and changed, and one stanza has been added by the famous hymn collector, Rev. John Rippon, in 1787.

Oh, that with yonder sacred throng
We at His feet may fall;
We’ll join the everlasting song,
And crown Him Lord of all.

As we wrap up this amazing story of the life of Edward Perronet and the others who have had their part in bringing this immortal hymn to us, let’s take a look in closing at the effect this hymn has had on heathens who knew nothing about Jesus. The most famous story connected with Perronet’s great hymn is told of the missionary to India, Rev. E.P. Scott. One day he saw on the street a man of so strange an appearance that he inquired about him and learned that he belonged to a wild mountain tribe among whom Christ had never been preached. Mr. Scott prayed over the matter and decided to visit that tribe. As soon as he reached their mountain home, he fell in among a savage band of murderous tribesmen who were on a war expedition, and who were closing in on him with their spears. They seized him and pointed their spears at his heart. At once the missionary drew out the violin that he always carried with him and began to play and sing in the native language, “All hail the power of Jesus’ name!” He closed his eyes, expecting death at any minute. When he reached the fourth stanza, and nothing had happened, he opened his eyes, and was amazed to see that the spears had fallen from the hands of the savages, and big tears were in their eyes! They invited Mr. Scott to their homes, and he spent the remaining years of his life preaching and ministering God’s love and redemption to these people. God in His providence used a simple hymn as a means of introducing the gospel to a group of needy pagans.

Du er verdig, Herre, til å få ære, ære og makt; for du skapte alle ting, og ved din vilje er de og ble de skapt – Åpenbaringen 4:11.

Denne salmen, ofte kalt «Kristendommens nasjonalsang», er kanskje en av de største salmene gjennom tidene. Den ble skrevet av Edward Perronet og sto først i Gospel Magazine i november 1779. Den ble redigert av Augustus Toplady, som også er forfatteren av en annen velkjent salme, «Rock of Ages». Teksten til denne salmen, All Hail the Power of Jesus Name, er blitt oversatt til nesten alle språk hvor kristendommen er kjent. Hvor enn den synges, treffer den menneskehjertets åndelige behov. En forfatter har sagt: «Så lenge det finnes kristne på jorden, vil den fortsette å bli sunget; og etter det, i himmelen.»

Edward Perronet ble født i Sundridge, Kent, England, i 1726. Han stammet fra en fremtredende fransk hugenottfamilie som hadde flyktet til Sveits og senere til England på grunn av den religiøse forfølgelsen i Frankrike. Edwards far, en prest i den engelske statskirken, hadde sterk sympati for den evangeliske bevegelsen ledet av Wesley-brødrene og George Whitefield. Edward ble, lik sin far, også prest i den anglikanske kirken, men var alltid kritisk til dens væremåte. En gang skrev han: «Jeg ble født og jeg kommer trolig til å dø i den vaklende kommunionen i den engelske kirke, men jeg forakter hennes tåpeligheter.» Snart brøt han imidlertid med kirken og engasjerte seg energisk i Wesley-brødrenes evangeliske arbeid på 1740- og 1750-tallet.

Charles Wesley skriver om Edward Perronets frimodighet i forkynnelsen. En gang ble han og Perronet beleiret i et hus av en mobb med grove skjennere, som Perronet møtte med mot mens de fornærmet ham og kastet jord på ham. Det var i denne tiden at Wesley-brødrene og deres tilhengere ble utsatt for mye forfølgelse og til og med vold fra dem som var uenige i deres tjeneste. Om disse erfaringene noterte Wesley i sin dagbok: «Fra Rockdale dro vi til Bolton, og snart fant vi at Rockdale-løvene var lammer sammenlignet med dem i Bolton.» Edward Perronet ble kastet ned og rullet i søle og gjørme. Steiner ble kastet og vinduer knust.

En annen interessant beretning gjelder forholdet mellom Wesley-brødrene og Perronet. John Wesley ønsket å høre Perronet forkynne, og Perronet, som var 18 år yngre enn John, hadde alltid nektet å forkynne i den eldre kirkemannens nærvær. Så en dag, da Wesley så Edward i menigheten, annonserte han at han ville preke ved neste samling. For å unngå en offentlig konflikt med Wesley gikk Perronet opp i prekestolen neste morgen, men forklarte raskt at han aldri hadde samtykket til å preke. «Likevel,» la han til, «vil jeg holde den største prekenen som noen gang er holdt på jorden.» Han leste så Bergprekenen og satte seg ned uten kommentar.

Etter åtte år med samarbeid med Wesley-brødrene førte Perronets stahet og frie ånd til en splittelse mellom dem, ettersom han var uenig i noen av deres regler. De fortsatte imidlertid å holde av hverandre og elske hverandre.

De siste årene av Perronets liv ble tilbrakt i Canterbury, hvor han var pastor for en uavhengig menighet, og hvor han døde i 1792, i en alder av sekstiseks år. Hans siste ord har også blitt klassiske: «Ære være Gud i høyden for Hans guddommelighet! Ære være Gud i dybden for Hans menneskelighet! Ære være Gud i Hans alt-tilstrekkelighet! I Hans hender overgir jeg min ånd.»

Selv om Perronet skrev mange andre salmer og diktformer, har ingen av dem oppnådd berømmelse bortsett fra den udødelige «All Hail the Power of Jesus Name». Tekstens suksess har utvilsomt blitt fremmet av tre gode melodier. «Coronation», komponert av Oliver Holden, en snekker fra Massachusetts, selvlært musiker og respektert sangskolelærer, er mest brukt i Amerika. «Miles Lane», komponert av William Shrubsole, Perronets personlige venn, er mest populær i Storbritannia. Mens den festlige «Diadem»-melodien, komponert i 1838 til denne teksten av James Ellor, en engelsk lekperson, ofte brukes som korstykke. Denne salmen ble opprinnelig skrevet med tittelen «On the Resurrection», og den hadde åtte vers, som følger:

All hail the power of Jesus’ name,
Let angels prostrate fall
Bring forth the royal diadem,
To crown Him Lord of all!

Let high born seraphs tune the lyre,
And, as they tune it, fall
Before His face who tunes their choir,
And crown Him Lord of all!

Crown Him, ye morning stars of light,
Who fixed this floating ball,
Now hail the Strength of Israel’s might,
And crown Him Lord of all!

Crown Him, ye martyrs of your God,
Who from His altar call;
Extol the stem of Jesse’s rod,
And crown Him Lord of all!

Ye seed of Israel’s chosen race,
Ye ransomed of the fall,
Hail Him who saves you by His grace
And crown Him Lord of all!

Hail Him, ye heirs of David’s line,
Whom David Lord did call.
The God incarnate, Man divine,
And crown Him Lord of all!

Sinners, whose love can ne’er forget
The wormwood and the gall,
Go spread your trophies at His feet,
And crown Him Lord of all!

Let every tribe and every tongue
That bound creation’s call
Now shout in universal song,
The crowned Lord of all!

Som den nå står i våre salmebøker, er salmen forkortet og endret, og ett vers ble lagt til av den berømte salmesamleren, prest John Rippon, i 1787.

Oh, that with yonder sacred throng
We at His feet may fall;
We’ll join the everlasting song,
And crown Him Lord of all.

Når vi avrunder denne bemerkelsesverdige beretningen om livet til Edward Perronet og de andre som har hatt sin del i å bringe denne udødelige salmen til oss, la oss til slutt se på hvilken virkning denne salmen har hatt på hedninger som ikke kjente til Jesus. Den mest berømte historien knyttet til Perronets store salme fortelles om misjonæren til India, Rev. E. P. Scott. En dag så han i gaten en mann med så merkelig utseende at han spurte om ham og fikk vite at han tilhørte en vill fjellstamme hvor Kristus aldri var blitt forkynt. Mr. Scott ba over saken og besluttet å besøke stammen. Så snart han nådde deres fjellhjem, falt han blant en vill bande av mordiske stammemenn som var på krigstokt, og som nærmet seg ham med spyd. De grep ham og pekte spyd mot hans hjerte. Med en gang tok misjonæren fram fiolinen han alltid bar med seg og begynte å spille og synge på morsmålet: «All hail the power of Jesus’ name!» Han lukket øynene, forventet å dø hvert øyeblikk. Da han nådde fjerde vers, og ingenting hadde skjedd, åpnet han øynene og ble forbauset over å se at spydene hadde falt fra de villmennenes hender, og store tårer fylte øynene deres! De inviterte Mr. Scott til hjemmene sine, og han tilbrakte de gjenværende årene av sitt liv med å forkynne og tjene Guds kjærlighet og forløsning for disse menneskene. Gud brukte i sin forsyn en enkel salme som et middel til å introdusere evangeliet for en gruppe trengende hedninger.
